flawed_step: Step 1 holds: cl(A∩B) ⊆ cl(A)∩cl(B). Because A∩B ⊆ A, A∩B ⊆ cl(A), and cl(A) is closed. So cl(A∩B) ⊆ cl(A). The same argument gives cl(A∩B) ⊆ cl(B). Step 2, the reverse inclusion cl(A)∩cl(B) ⊆ cl(A∩B), cannot be justified. A point can be a limit of A and also a limit of B without being a limit of points that lie in both A and B. In general, closure does not commute with intersections.
counterexample: Take X = ℝ with the standard topology, A = (0,1) and B = (1,2). Then A∩B = ∅, so cl(A∩B) = ∅. But cl(A) = [0,1] and cl(B) = [1,2], so cl(A)∩cl(B) = {1}. Since {1} ≠ ∅, the equality fails.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. Only the inclusion cl(A∩B) ⊆ cl(A)∩cl(B) holds in general. The reverse inclusion fails, for example with A=(0,1) and B=(1,2) in ℝ: the closure of the intersection is ∅, but the intersection of the closures is {1}.
